title: Conjecture 1.1 (Aravind)
statement_text: Let $G$ be a triangle-free graph. Then for every colouring (not necessarily optimal) of $G$, there is a rainbow induced subgraph isomorphic to a $\chi(G)$-vertex path.
context_text: This conjecture, due to Aravind (cited via Babu, Basavaraju, Chandran and Francis), asks for the strongest possible rainbow induced path result in triangle-free graphs. It remains open; partial results include the case $\chi(G)=4$ and a version for graphs whose girth equals their chromatic number.
paper_contribution: Proves Theorem 1.3, a weaker statement in which the path length $s$ is fixed in advance rather than equal to $\chi(G)$: for every $\kappa, s \geq 1$ there exists $c$ such that every coloured graph $(G,\phi)$ with $\omega(G)\leq\kappa$ and $\chi(G)>c$ contains a rainbow induced $s$-vertex path. The authors also explicitly state they do not believe Conjecture 1.1, and report an unsuccessful search for a counterexample on the Mycielski graph with $\chi(G)=5$.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. IX. Rainbow paths

title: Question (rainbow hole with $s$ consecutive rainbow vertices)
statement_text: Is it true that for all fixed $s$, $\kappa$, if $G$ is a graph with $\omega(G)\leq\kappa$ and $\chi(G)$ sufficiently large, then in every colouring of $G$ there is a hole in which some set of $s$ consecutive vertices is rainbow?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A colouring of $G$ is any proper colouring (not necessarily optimal), and a subgraph is rainbow if its vertices receive pairwise distinct colours. The authors prove that for all $\kappa,s\ge1$ there is $c$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)\le\kappa$ and $\chi(G)>c$ and every colouring of $G$, some $s$-vertex induced path is rainbow (extending Gyárfás and Sárközy, who assumed girth at least five). A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four. Asking for a fully rainbow hole fails: in the shift graph of triples (vertex set the $3$-subsets of $[n]$, two triples adjacent if the two smallest elements of one are the two largest of the other), which is triangle-free with large chromatic number, colouring each triple by its middle element gives a colouring with no hole in which every three consecutive vertices are rainbow, since every rainbow three-vertex path is monotone and cannot close up into a cycle. The question is whether some set of $s$ consecutive vertices of a hole can always be made rainbow. The authors note that every graph with bounded clique number and large enough chromatic number does at least contain a long hole (resolving an old conjecture of Gyárfás).
notes: Stated as prose in the Conclusion with 'we do not know the following'.

title: Question (uniquely-covered vertices in an induced path)
statement_text: Let $G$ be a triangle-free graph with very large chromatic number, and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a set of stable subsets (not necessarily pairwise disjoint) of $V(G)$ with union $V(G)$. Does there necessarily exist an $s$-vertex induced path $P$ of $G$ such that for each $v\in V(P)$, some $X\in\mathcal{A}$ satisfies $X\cap V(P)=\{v\}$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A colouring of $G$ is any proper colouring (not necessarily optimal), and a subgraph is rainbow if its vertices receive pairwise distinct colours. The authors prove that for all $\kappa,s\ge1$ there is $c$ such that for every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)\le\kappa$ and $\chi(G)>c$ and every colouring of $G$, some $s$-vertex induced path is rainbow (extending Gyárfás and Sárközy, who assumed girth at least five). In this question $s$ is fixed and the chromatic number of $G$ is very large in terms of $s$. A stable set is a set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices. If $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of colour classes of a proper colouring, the required property says exactly that $P$ is rainbow, so a positive answer would extend the authors' theorem (for triangle-free graphs) from partitions into stable sets to arbitrary covers by stable sets.
notes: Stated as prose in the Conclusion with 'another question to which we do not know the answer'.
